analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting health coverage for workers on strike or locked out.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in June 2025 and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to make it an illegal employer practice to terminate or change an employee's health insurance under a group health plan while the employer is locking workers out or while employees are on a lawful strike. Employers who cut coverage anyway would face civil penalties starting at $50,000–$75,000 per violation, doubled for repeat offenders in serious cases, with possible personal liability for executives. It was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who go on strike or are locked out during a labor dispute. Under current practice, employers can cut off health coverage during a strike or lockout, forcing workers to choose between their job action and their family's medical insurance. This bill would keep coverage in place for the duration of the dispute and impose penalties on employers who violate it, including officers who knew of a violation and did nothing.

how_it_helps.text: It adds new unfair labor practices to the National Labor Relations Act, making it illegal for an employer to terminate or alter an employee's group health plan coverage while locking out workers or while employees are on a lawful strike.

It creates civil penalties of up to $50,000–$75,000 per violation, doubled for repeat employers whose actions cause serious economic harm, and allows penalties against individual directors and officers who directed or knew of the violation.
It applies regardless of which side initiates the dispute: it covers lockouts as well as strikes, so workers withholding labor and workers locked out by management get the same protection.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with unionized workforces, who would have to keep paying their share of health premiums during a strike or lockout and would face civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation—doubled for repeat offenders in serious cases—if they cut coverage anyway.

drawbacks.text: Employers would have to keep paying their share of health plan costs during a strike or lockout even while receiving no work from those employees, a genuine added expense, particularly for small employers in a prolonged dispute.

The bill stacks new civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation (doubled for repeat offenders) and opens the door to personal liability for corporate directors and officers, on top of existing NLRB remedies; opponents of expanded National Labor Relations Board penalties argue this escalates litigation risk for employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is large: it removes the single most dangerous consequence of striking or being locked out—losing health coverage. The costs are real but narrow: employers continuing coverage during disputes face added expense, and critics argue the penalties tilt bargaining leverage toward unions. On balance the bill addresses a targeted, well-defined hardship rather than rewriting labor law broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no hearing, vote, or floor action followed.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on June 5, 2025, joined by ten original cosponsors.
Fourteen senators, all Democrats or Independents, had signed on as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no committee vote, no floor debate, no roll call.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use the threat of losing health coverage as leverage in labor disputes are better off, because the bill has not advanced. Workers on strike or locked out remain exposed to losing their health insurance.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its penalty provisions for employers who cut health coverage during strikes and lockouts.

for.name: 14 Senate cosponsors (13 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Senate cosponsors including Sanders, Warren, Fetterman, Blumenthal, Padilla, Durbin, Smith, Whitehouse, Markey, Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

against.name: Business and employer lobbies
against.role: Employer associations (e.g., U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
against.what_they_did: Oppose mandates on employers during labor disputes as a matter of general position; no documented action on this specific bill in the provided sources.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors are Democrats or the Independent from Vermont; no Republican has signed on, so the bill's path in a Senate that needs 60 votes to advance most legislation is narrow.

industries.note: Companies would have to keep funding health coverage for striking or locked-out employees and would face new civil penalties for cutting it off, including possible personal liability for executives.

industries.industry: Employer-sponsored health insurers and plan administrators
industries.note: Coverage during strikes and lockouts would continue, keeping premium revenue flowing through employer plans, but the industry gains no new protections.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action six months after introduction, the bill is likely to die in committee at the end of the 119th Congress unless labor policy moves up the agenda or a discharge petition is attempted, which is rare for a first-term bill from a single party.
